title: The emperor's questions
hookLine: Heraclius questions Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, and Abu Sufyan can't bring himself to lie
carry: even his enemy told the truth

cards: A trade caravan from Mecca is doing business in Syria during the truce. With it is Abu Sufyan, a leader of the Prophet's opponents.
A summons arrives: the Roman emperor, Heraclius, wants to question these Arabs, and asks which of them is the closest relative of the man who claims to be a prophet. Abu Sufyan is.

So he stands in a royal court, with an interpreter, in front of an emperor. Behind him the emperor places Abu Sufyan's companions, and tells them: if he lies to me, say so. Today: the emperor's questions.

teach.h: ONE PLAIN QUESTION AT A TIME.
teach.b: This report sits in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter on how revelation began, in Abu Sufyan's own telling. Heraclius asks about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, one plain question at a time.
What is his family like among you? Has anyone among you made this claim before him? Do his followers come from the powerful, or the weak?
Are they growing or shrinking? Does anyone leave his religion out of resentment? Did you ever accuse him of lying before he made this claim?
Does he break his word? What does he tell you to do? And here's the line that makes the story.

teach.h: HE WOULD HAVE LIED, BUT FOR SHAME.
teach.b: Abu Sufyan admits that if he hadn't been afraid of his companions reporting him as a liar, he would have lied. But they were right behind him. So he answered straight.
He says the only place he could slip in a little doubt was this: we're in a truce with him now, and we don't know what he'll do in it. Then Heraclius goes back through every answer.
A man who never lied about people, he reasons, would not start lying about God. The weak are the ones who follow messengers. Messengers don't betray.

teach.h: THE ANSWERS DRAW AN HONEST MAN.
teach.b: One answer after another, the enemy's own testimony draws a picture of an honest man. That's the strange gift in this story. Abu Sufyan didn't come to praise anyone.

teach.h: EVEN HIS ENEMY TOLD THE TRUTH.
teach.b: He came cornered, with his own companions at his back, and the truth came out of him anyway.

how: Muslims read the Heraclius report near the start of Sahih al-Bukhari, and it is retold as an account of the Prophet's character given by someone who was then his opponent.

o: the Roman emperor who questioned Abu Sufyan
the Christian king of Abyssinia who sheltered Muslims
a Greek philosopher whose books reached Mecca

games.q: the emperor's questions — tap the pairs.
p: stood behind him as a check
we don't know what he'll do in the truce

s: Abu Sufyan was a follower of the Prophet at the time
he was one of his opponents, trading in Syria during the truce.
Abu Sufyan admitted he would have lied if he could
only the fear of being reported as a liar kept him straight.
Heraclius asked whether his followers were growing
he asked if they were growing or shrinking, and whether anyone left out of resentment.

games.q: you're Abu Sufyan, in front of an emperor, asked about your enemy. your companions stand behind you. what do you do?
o: lie, and make him look bad.
answer straight, slipping in one small doubt.
games.why: he answered honestly, afraid of being called a liar, and slipped in only one doubt: we don't know what he'll do in the truce.

practice: Bring to mind someone you compete with, or simply don't like, and ask a few of the emperor's plain questions about them: do they keep their word? Do they lie?

Answer honestly, the way Abu Sufyan had to, with someone standing behind you, and notice where you'd like to slip in a little doubt. If you pray, you can ask Allah to keep your tongue truthful about the people you find hard.

wordCard.voice: Heraclius, the Roman emperor who questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, and whose own reasoning, drawn from an enemy's testimony, described an honest man. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Heraclius, the Roman emperor, as he is named in the report.

carryVoice: Your line: even his enemy told the truth. Honest answers drew an honest man. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (Kitab Bad' al-Wahy, the report of Heraclius)
